title: The Way to Preserve Wealth
author: Nie Yuntai
excerpt: The author of The Way to Preserve Wealth, Mr. Nie Yuntai, was a grandson of the eminent Qing official Zeng Guofan and the first president of the Shanghai Chamber of Commerce. Drawing on his own family's experience and on the changes he witnessed in the households of the rich in Shanghai, he discusses how a prosperous family may endure and flourish. It is well worth reading, especially today.

inline.s: About This Book:

The author of The Way to Preserve Wealth, Mr. Nie Yuntai, was a grandson of the eminent Qing official Zeng Guofan and the first president of the Shanghai Chamber of Commerce. Drawing on his own family's experience and on the changes he witnessed in the households of the rich in Shanghai, he discusses how a prosperous family may endure and flourish. It is well worth reading, especially today.
This essay was published in the Shenbao and caused a sensation in Shanghai; for a time people from every walk of life vied with one another in donating generously to support students.
Master Yinguang, Liu Yazi, and other eminent men of Buddhist learning wrote articles strongly recommending it.
People took it upon themselves to print and give the book away, and to this day it still circulates widely among merchants in Hong Kong, Taiwan, and Southeast Asia.

blocks.text: Foreword One: A Letter to Upasaka Nie Yuntai (Vernacular Rendering)

inline.s: Master Yinguang

I have received and read your family letters, and my admiration is beyond words. It appears that you have truly inherited Wenzheng Gong's (that is, Zeng Guofan's — translator's note) inner method of conducting himself and dealing with the world. Thus you are able to rise above the habits of the rich and noble, to delight in your own innocent nature, and not to be turned about by material desires. What you wrote in your letter to a certain gentleman is indeed a wonderful remedy for rousing people's hearts and lifting them out of despondency, but I fear that gentleman has no such aspiration, and so it can have no effect. Still, if this letter were made public, there would certainly be those willing to follow its example. If people could, through the comings and goings of wealth that you set forth, go further and understand deeply the workings of cause, condition, and karmic reward in every aspect of life, then the realm of the sages and worthies would not be hard to reach. Your letter is therefore truly a masterpiece for the salvation of the age. From this we know that to make the law of cause and effect clear to the world brings benefits to living beings that are deep and far-reaching. Those who dismiss the law of cause and effect as a mere provisional, gradual, Hinayana teaching are all people who deal in hearsay.

I have often said that to set forth the law of cause and effect, of good and evil, is the best method by which the sages of the world and beyond the world govern the realm and deliver living beings. In the present age, unless we begin by making clear the retribution of cause and effect, then even if all the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, sages, and worthies were to appear in the world together, there would be no way to save the morals of the age and the hearts of men. I also hold that the education of children is the foremost task in governing a state and bringing peace to the world, and the education of girls above all. For more than half the power to govern the state and pacify the world lies in the hands of the world's women. How do we know? That the world has few worthy men is because the world has few worthy women. Where there are worthy women, there are worthy wives and good mothers. Where there are worthy wives and good mothers, then among their husbands and children there will seldom be any who are unworthy. Those who advocate that women must be the same as men in every respect truly do not understand the affairs of the world. One should know that men have men's powers and women have women's powers. To assist her husband and teach her children is woman's heaven-ordained duty, and this power is in truth very, very great. The above are my shallow views; I do not know what you think of them. If you do not consider them perverse, I would venture to ask you to expound and proclaim these principles at length, for it may well prove of some help in restoring the morals of the age and the hearts of men.

blocks.text: Foreword Two: A Practitioner of the Way to Preserve Wealth

inline.s: Liu Yazi

Ever since Mr. Nie Yuntai's The Way to Preserve Wealth appeared in the Shenbao, it was passed from household to household and recited in every home; there is no telling how many people it moved. Yet it is not yet known how many of the wealthy have actually put it into practice. For such things are easy to speak of, but when the time for practice arrives, difficulties are unavoidable. As the saying goes, "To know is not hard; to act is hard." We need not discuss this now; in time it will be made clear enough.

What I wish to introduce to you now is a man of the distant Ming dynasty who practiced the way to preserve wealth. His conduct is well worth studying. In Zhang Dafu's Collected Writings of the Plum Blossom Thatched Cottage there is this record: "In Sichuan there was an official serving as provincial judge who had five sons. To each son he assigned an estate just sufficient for food and warmth, and he himself was frugal in food and clothing. In his old age he took out the salary he had saved over a lifetime — as much as ten thousand in gold — and offered it to make up any shortfall in the public funds. The local officials said there was nothing that needed to be made up. He then had the ten thousand in gold buried in an old courtyard, covered it with stone slabs, and inscribed on them: 'Returned to the Creator.' After his death no one touched this treasure vault. In the xinyou year of the Wanli reign, bandits rose in revolt and plundered all public and private property. Local officials and people alike faced starvation. Someone who knew of the vault reported it to the authorities, and the wealth was used to relieve the people of that place. The lofty virtue of this old man is truly rare in a thousand ages. Even the officials and common people of that place at that time were thoroughly upright."

Readers may laugh at this old gentleman for being too foolish — why bury money in a cellar at all? My own view is that in those days there were perhaps no charitable organizations; he had wanted to give the money to the public authorities, and they would not accept it. At such a point another man might have changed his original intention and divided the property among his sons after all, and no one could have called him inconsistent. For the money truly had nowhere to go. Yet this old gentleman looked upon that sum as he would a venomous snake or a savage beast, and would on no account allow it to remain in his children's hands. Rather than bequeath a calamity a hundred generations long to his descendants, he would ask leave to dig a pit in a ruined courtyard and store it there. Reading this, we cannot but admire his far-seeing judgment; it is truly beyond the reach of ordinary men of wealth. He understood the principle of the way to preserve wealth through and through, not merely its surface, and so once he had made up his mind he would never change it.

In reading The Way to Preserve Wealth, we too should ponder carefully the truth it sets forth. If one reading does not make it quite clear, we may as well read it several times over, until we understand it thoroughly. Then, when the time comes to act, we will feel no hesitation at all. People die for wealth; better to devote oneself to works of public benefit, profiting both self and others — that is the great way to leave a good name to later ages.

blocks.text: Foreword Three: A Warning to Those Clever at Acquiring Wealth

inline.s: Ding Fubao

Every word of Mr. Yuntai's The Way to Preserve Wealth flows from the depths of his heart. A few days ago, Mr. Huang Jingwan submitted the manuscript to the Shenbao; within a few days, readers had contributed more than four hundred and seventy-five thousand yuan to the Shenbao Readers' Student Aid Fund. So great is the power of this book to move and transform its readers.

In the past, Mr. Lu Yi of Taicang said: "Heaven is jealous of talent, and still more jealous of wealth; if a man has both talent and wealth, and that wealth is not what his own lot entitles him to, then extraordinary disaster cannot be far away. I once saw such a case with my own eyes, and so I know this principle to be exact and unerring. There was a man who, within a few years of passing the metropolitan examination, was appointed to high office with his own secretariat and put in charge of the state finances, and he was very famous at the time. His son in turn held office at the same court. For a while the world envied that family greatly. But before long two of his grandsons died young, then his only son died, and then the great official himself passed away. In less than half a year three generations were extinguished, leaving only a lady of over ninety, whose grief was beyond words; she could not even speak when she met people, and could only shed tears. Think back to when this great official was at court: every year he sent messengers to all parts to demand the customary annual levy — a disguised form of extortion — speaking in the most earnest terms, even stooping to words about official appointments and promises. People felt they could not refuse out of courtesy, and most scraped together what was demanded. In this way the wealth he accumulated over the years was beyond counting. In fact this great official had no power to promote or dismiss anyone; he merely borrowed the influence of his position at court and deliberately put on a pitiable air, all for the sake of getting money. Once the money was in hand, whether the matter was accomplished or not, no one could reproach him, and so he could enjoy his wealth in peace. Such a scheme was exceedingly clever — truly a case of talent and wealth together. Yet in a flash he let go of everything and departed, unable to carry so much as a penny with him below the earth. The gods of heaven and earth help those who sincerely do good, keeping it as far as possible from people's knowledge; and for those who do evil in secret, they make it known to all the world. To do good without others knowing is hidden virtue, and its future reward is sure to be abundant. This great official was clever at acquiring wealth and kept his schemes from being known, which is precisely the opposite of accumulating hidden virtue; no wonder his retribution was so severe. Though the old lady is still in distress, and it seems one should not speak of this man's shameful deeds, yet to awaken those who are clever at acquiring wealth I shall write it out as a warning from the cart ahead."

If this great official had applied the principles set out in The Way to Preserve Wealth and scattered his accumulated wealth among the poor, he could certainly have turned extraordinary disaster into immense blessing. In recent years many have made sudden fortunes; whoever wishes to avoid repeating this great official's fate must first read The Way to Preserve Wealth! Those with deep roots of goodness will believe as soon as they read it and will put it into practice; those with heavy karmic obstructions may not believe even after reading, and I fear would not heed it even if the author himself reminded them to their face.

People of this age for the most part do not understand the principles of the dark and the bright, the hidden and the manifest, and think that when a person dies there is no ghost, that all is annihilated. Therefore in life, whatever the matter, so long as it benefits themselves for the moment, they will do it even if it harms others; or though the harm others suffer exceeds their own gain a thousandfold, they feel no scruple at all. Thus every kind of monstrous evil — seizing others' wealth for oneself, trampling others down to exalt oneself, cutting short others' lives to prolong one's own, and all the ten evil deeds of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech — they boldly commit. They do not know that when their allotted span is exhausted, all the vengeful ghosts of those they wronged in life come to demand their lives, and after death they go together before King Yama for judgment; every advantage gained in life, every dark deed committed, must be repaid one by one, whether by falling into the hells, or into the realms of hungry ghosts or animals. The karmic retribution they receive matches the ten evil deeds committed in life in weight and measure as exactly as five sparrows and six swallows (from the Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art

'Fangcheng' chapter: 'Now there are five sparrows and six swallows; they are placed together on the balance, and the sparrows are all heavy while the swallows are all light; let one sparrow and one swallow be exchanged, and the balance is exactly level.' — a figure for the two sides being equal in weight.)

In writing this preface I have set out in brief the facts of cause and effect and of reincarnation, in order to exhort the people of the world. Mr. Yuntai, I am sure, will agree from the bottom of his heart.
Respectfully prefaced by Ding Fubao of Wuxi on April 4, 1943, in his seventieth year.

In middle age the lay Buddhist Nie Yuntai studied the Buddhadharma and called upon Master Yinguang, penetrating the profound meaning of the Mahayana; then, turning from Buddhism back to the affairs of the world, in

he wrote The Way to Preserve Wealth, which was serialized in Shanghai's Shenbao and stirred the hearts of his contemporaries. Within a few days, people from every walk of life in Shanghai donated more than four hundred and seventy thousand yuan for student aid. Liu Yazi and other notables responded one after another, and for a time it was praised on every side. In the book he lays bare the true meaning of life and sees through to the very source of wealth. Though the book is titled 'Preserving Wealth,' it in fact calls on people to give up wealth for the sake of goodness. It urges the people of the world to understand the giving away of wealth in charity, and to cultivate merit and virtue. Only by deeply believing in cause and effect, by nurturing merit and opening the source, and by knowing how to cherish one's blessings — treasuring one's good fortune and broadening one's heart — can one best preserve one's blessings and one's wealth. Master Yinguang, Liu Yazi, and other eminent figures of the Buddhist world wrote articles urging it upon readers, praising it as a marvelous piece for admonishing people's hearts.

blocks.text: The Way to Preserve Wealth: Part One

inline.s: As the saying goes: to make a fortune is not hard; to keep it is hardest of all. I have lived in Shanghai for more than fifty years and have seen many people make their fortunes. Of these, some declined within five or ten years, some within twenty or thirty, and some ran through everything in forty or fifty years. I remember that most of the wealthy men who associated with my late father — some officials, some merchants — were for a time immensely powerful, yet today most have withered away and their family fortunes have fallen into ruin. Some were squandered to nothing because their descendants frequented brothels and gambling houses and would not take up honest work; of others, even the descendants have vanished without a trace. Roughly reckoned, among the wealthy of forty or fifty years ago, of those whose property has not been entirely lost, and whose descendants can still study, work honestly, and strive to improve, there is scarcely one or two households in a hundred.

It is not only Shanghai that is so; in my native Hunan the same holds true. Among the rich and noble of the Tongzhi and Guangxu reigns of the Qing — the era of restoration — there were six or seven families holding noble titles, twenty or thirty serving as governors-general and governors, and fifty or sixty as provincial military commanders; today most of them too have fallen into decline. Only a few civil officials' families of modest means are left, whose descendants have fared comparatively well. Among those I know well, families such as the Zeng (Zeng Guofan), the Zuo (Zuo Zongtang), the Peng (Peng Yulin), and the Li (Li Hongzhang) were the high officials with the least money, and their descendants have more often been able to study and to serve society through learning: among the great-grandsons of Zeng Wenzheng Gong (Zeng Guofan), six or seven graduated from universities at home or abroad, and three became university professors; several great-grandsons of Zuo Wengxiang Gong (Zuo Zongtang) are likewise known for their scientific expertise; among the grandsons of Li Yongyi Gong (Li Hongzhang) there are university professors, and most of his great-grandsons are university graduates; and among the descendants of Peng Gangzhi Gong (Peng Yulin) there were, ten years ago, those serving as officials in Shanghai.

Wherever the money of that time came by honest means, and there was no wish to hoard it up for one's descendants, the descendants tended to be worthy and capable. Of the dozen or so civil officials' families that were relatively rich, most of their descendants today have declined; and of the several dozen military officials' families, all richer at the time than the civil officials, with a hundred thousand or two hundred thousand taels of silver, most of their descendants have likewise fallen away; of those able to study and advance themselves, one hears very little.

My family was linked by ties of friendship across the generations to most of the great houses of the late Qing restoration era, whether of the Hunan or the Huai army faction, and so I have some knowledge of how each rose and fell. As for the great civil and military families of Anhui, once far wealthier than the men of the Hunan army, today they have all withered and fallen, too painful to look back upon; in the space of only a few decades, by the third generation, they have scattered like drifting clouds. Yet the few families that would not seek wealth and would not pile up money for their descendants — their descendants, on the contrary, have mostly been outstanding and distinguished.

The clearest case is Zeng Wenzheng Gong. His position was the highest and his power the greatest, yet after twenty years in office he had only twenty thousand taels of silver when he died; apart from the old family house in the countryside, he never built a single room in the provincial capital, nor bought a single acre of land. The Lianghuai salt certificates that he himself created were priced very low while carrying extremely high interest; each certificate cost two hundred taels and later sold for twenty thousand, yielding three or four thousand taels in annual interest. In those days a family with even one salt certificate could be called well-to-do. Yet Zeng Wenzheng Gong issued a special order that no member of the Zeng family was permitted to take one out; for many years after his death his descendants still held not a single certificate. Had they simply used a few trade names and assumed names at the time, obtaining one or two hundred certificates would have been extremely easy; and since the certificates were issued according to the regulations, on the surface it would not have been illegal. But to use political power and position for clever self-seeking — the petty man thinks it does no harm to his conscience, while the gentleman will have none of it! My mother knew the details of this matter very well, while outsiders scarcely knew of it at all. The Doctrine of the Mean says: "What the gentleman cannot be matched in is that which others do not see."

Wenzheng Gong once swore an oath before his subordinates (his colleagues and juniors): "I will not take a single coin from the army and send it home," and for decades he kept that oath as faithfully as on the first day; in this he was of one style with Duke Zhuge of the Three Kingdoms period (Zhuge Liang). For this reason most of the generals and officials of that time were thoroughly honest, and the common people benefited not a little, though imperceptibly. So it is that when those in office practice integrity themselves, they secretly bring blessings to the people; but if they themselves covet money, then every general and official beneath them wants to get rich, and the common people suffer no small harm.

The Great Learning says: "The benevolent man uses wealth to perfect his person; the unbenevolent man uses his person to amass wealth." (One who is benevolent uses wealth to develop and perfect himself; one who is not benevolent uses himself to amass wealth.) Mencius says: "Those who grow rich are not benevolent; those who are benevolent do not grow rich." (The commentary says: "The rich delight in hoarding, the benevolent delight in giving; the one who gives cannot hoard, for their ways are opposed.") For whether or not one covets wealth bears on the interests and happiness of others; therefore to grow rich can create offense, and only by not coveting wealth can one create blessings. The world believes that by piling up money and buying more land and houses one can ensure that one's descendants will have food to eat and live happily, and so people strive desperately to get rich. Look now at the facts of those dozens of families: those who piled up the most money in fact left their descendants without food, and even cut off their descendants altogether; while those who would not get rich by clever means saw their descendants fed and flourishing. Ordinary people also think that without some savings their descendants will at once fall into poverty; yet from the facts of history and the experience of society, if a person truly benefits others and thinks nothing of himself, keeping not a single coin, his descendants are sure to prosper. Let me now give a few more examples.

Fan Wenzheng Gong (Fan Zhongyan) of the Song dynasty had his heart set on relieving others even when he was a poor scholar. Later, when he became prime minister, he took out his entire salary to buy charitable estates for the support of the poor of his clan. He first bought the Southern Garden in Suzhou for his own residence, but afterward, hearing a geomancer say, "The feng shui of this house is excellent; your descendants will produce ministers and nobles," he thought: since this house will bring prominence and honor, better to turn it into a school where the sons of all Suzhou may be educated, so that many more may rise to prominence and honor — that would be far better. So he at once donated the house as a school. His every thought was to benefit the many, and he was unwilling that his own family alone should have the advantage. In the end his four sons all rose to prominence and honor, serving as prime ministers, nobles, and vice ministers, and each was a model of lofty virtue. His sons once asked him to buy a garden estate in the capital so that he might enjoy it in retirement; he replied: "There are many gardens in the households of the great officials of the capital, and their owners cannot stroll in them often themselves — so who would forbid me to stroll there? Why must I have a garden of my own to take pleasure in?"

The young gentlemen of Fan Wenzheng Gong's household wore plain cotton clothes at home. In several decades as a general and a minister, all the salary Fan received was spent in charity and relief, so that his household was extremely frugal, and at his death there was not even enough to cover the funeral expenses. In the ordinary way of thinking this shows far too little regard for one's descendants — yet who would guess that this is the very best way to provide for them? Not only did all four sons become ministers and nobles; they were able to carry on their father's purpose of giving up wealth to relieve others. Thus the great-grandsons of the Fan family also prospered greatly, and the line has come down through some dozens of generations. To this day, eight hundred years later, there are still many descendants of the Fan family around the Fan graves in Suzhou, and outstanding offspring still appear from time to time. If people of the world wish to provide for their descendants, to leave them food and accumulate blessings, then let them act according to Fan Wenzheng Gong's intentions — that is the best method of all.

Next, Yelu Wenzheng Gong (Yelu Chucai) of the Yuan dynasty was the strategist of Yuan Taizu (Genghis Khan) and of Yuan Shizu; most military decisions were his to make, and through them he saved countless common people. Because Yuan Taizu was fond of killing, Yelu, being skilled with words, was able to dissuade him from massacre. Though he was a prime minister, he wore coarse cloth and ate plain food, living most frugally. He was a great Buddhist scholar, and his desire for profit was exceedingly faint. When Yanjing was taken, the other generals all went to the treasuries to seize treasure, while he merely ordered that several dozen piculs of rhubarb from the stores be sent to his camp. Before long a plague broke out, and he used the rhubarb to treat the sickness with great success. He too left no savings at all, yet among his descendants thirteen served as prime ministers over several generations. This is another proof that one who refuses to hoard private money may instead see his descendants greatly prosper.

Then there is Lin Wenzhong Gong (Lin Zexu) of the Qing dynasty, the great man who opposed British aggression and so brought on the Opium War. Had he wished to get rich, it would have been easy enough to lay hands on several million at the time. He held that opium was doing the people the gravest harm, and so he did not shrink from the drastic measure of burning twenty thousand chests of it. Later the British attacked Guangdong and could not take it for a year, but afterward they took Ningbo and Zhenjiang. The Qing court had no choice but to strip Lin Wenzhong Gong of his office and send him into exile, apologizing to the British and suing for peace. After Lin's death he too left no savings, yet for several generations his descendants kept up the family's scholarly tradition; among his great-grandsons there were still metropolitan and provincial graduates, and some remain distinguished to this day. Lin Xiang, chief justice of the Supreme Court, who died a few years ago, was one of them, and a man of most lofty character besides. This is yet another proof that one who refuses to get rich may instead see his descendants greatly prosper.

Look again at those who made great fortunes at the same time as Lin. I can give a few examples: the Wu, Pan, and Kong families of Guangdong all made vast fortunes, several million taels, out of the opium trade. Painters and calligraphers know well that most of the famous old calligraphies, paintings, and rubbings in the land bear the seals of the Wu, Pan, and Kong families, showing that the pieces were once in the collections of those three houses — so wealthy were they. Yet a few decades later these precious objects had passed into other hands. Their nanmu-wood houses were long ago torn down and became ornament and furniture in other households. Among their descendants there is not one of any note. The heads of these three families were, after all, shrewd and capable men, and that is how they made such great fortunes. Lin Wenzhong Gong (Lin Zexu) of that day had wealth within his reach but would not take it, and in the end brought dismissal and punishment upon himself — surely a great fool! And yet, looking at their descendants several decades on, one sees that Lin Wenzhong Gong was the wisest man in the world, while the Wu, Pan, and Kong families were the most foolish of all.

Shanghai has many great men of wealth. Among those I have known I can likewise give a few examples. One is Mr. Zhou of Jiangxi. Fifty years ago, at the Xiao family home in Yangzhou — my wife's family — I came to know this rich man (at that time both families were leaders among the salt merchants). One day Mr. Zhou came to the Xiao house in a fury: he had received a letter from the manager of their Xiangtan branch saying that a famine had struck Hunan, that the authorities were soliciting donations, and that the manager had pledged five hundred taels of silver on his employer's behalf. Mr. Zhou was angry that he had acted on his own authority and given too much. At the time he was worth several million taels, and yet he grudged five hundred taels for famine relief. Later, when he lived in Shanghai, Mr. Tan Zu'an (Tan Yankai, who served as chairman of the National Government and president of the Executive Yuan) sat at the same table with him one day and asked how he had grown so enormously rich. He said there was no other way: one simply accumulates and does not spend. He lived to be over eighty, leaving an estate of thirty million yuan; his descendants divided it into ten branches, and in a little over ten years it was all gone. One branch among them did a little good, and that branch fared somewhat better, though it too met with various unexpected losses and has not much left. By any ordinary reckoning, each branch should have had three million, and they could not all have gone to ruin so fast; yet in fact that is how they declined. If you ask how they ruined themselves, the reader may try closing his eyes and thinking of the ways a rich young man of Shanghai spends money — that will make it clear, and no more need be said. This old gentleman too was engaged in legitimate business and did not take what was not his due; but inwardly he was miserly and greedy, and when famine stared him in the face he would not give money for relief, thinking it clever to hoard and not spend. He did not know that such a mindset runs wholly counter to the good Dharma of kindness and equality. If I hold to the thought of being the one rich family and care nothing whether other families live or die, that is unkindness and inequality of the most extreme kind. Besides suffering karmic retribution himself, such a man comes under the sway of residual retribution — what the I Ching calls 'surplus blessings' and 'surplus calamities' — so that the family that alone grows rich declines with special speed, and the multitude, seeing the retribution with their own eyes, may awaken.

Another family: the Shanghai land king Mr. Chen of a dozen years ago, whose property amounted to forty million silver dollars, divided two thousand each between two branches of brothers. In 1925 I dined once at his house. The mansion he lived in was exceedingly splendid, with a pair of stone lions before the gate such as one seldom sees in Shanghai. In his guest hall the walls on all four sides were fitted with glass shelves, on which were displayed bronze ding vessels, all of them antiquities three thousand years old. One of the guests pointed to these antiques and told me: "The bronzes in this one room are worth a million and a half silver dollars; half of China's famous ancient bronzes are here." These were precisely the words the host most delighted to hear. The psychology of the rich, you see, is to boast that everything they have surpasses everyone else's. But virtue, reputation, and learning cannot be bought with money, and these rich men have no way to obtain them; so they can only vie with one another in clothes, jewels, houses, and implements, earning the flattery and deference of guests who hope for favors. Only seven years after I saw him, Shanghai land prices suddenly collapsed, and with losses from speculation he went bankrupt. The Chen family's ancient bronzes, treasures, houses, and land — everything — was confiscated and sold off by the banks, and the master himself moved back to his native place in the interior.

One more instance: the owner of the Hardoon Garden in Shanghai, about whom the newspapers have lately carried satirical comment — that in all their lives they would not give generously to charitable causes, and that he left an estate of eight hundred million silver dollars. Consider: on a fortune of eight hundred million, even at an interest of two percent a year, the income should be sixteen million a year. If they were willing to take the odd six million of that and use it to relieve the poor, every refugee in Shanghai could be saved. Three years ago there were a hundred thousand people in Shanghai's refugee shelters; reckoning each person's food at two yuan a month, the whole year came to only a little over two million. By last year, when rice was dear, the refugees in the shelters numbered only ten-odd thousand, each costing thirty yuan a month, some five or six million for the year — still only a third of the annual interest on their income. Then consider the poor who died in Shanghai's streets: last year nearly twenty thousand, the year before only ten-odd thousand, and the year before that only a few thousand. Take last year alone, when rice was dear and the deaths were the most: had a few shelters for the cold and gruel stations been set up, keeping those twenty or thirty thousand people alive would have cost only five or six million for the year. To the rich this is no more than a drop in the bucket — and yet that one drop they could not bear to give. A few million spent could have saved tens of thousands of the poor. As for their own household expenses, had there been no extraordinary extravagance, however freely they spent, they could still have saved the ten million or more in interest left over each year. In this way they would have won a fine reputation on the one hand, performed the great merit of saving lives on the other, and still added several million to their savings every year. Such a reckoning is perfectly sound. But they had no such wise vision; their whole mind was set on receiving those sixteen million a year without losing a drop, all into their own bank account, to be their own, to squander as they pleased. It never occurred to them that this fleshly body must die, and that having no children of their own, their property would in the end all pass to others. A fortune of hundreds of millions turns in an instant into a flower in the air, and they carry nothing away but a body full of karmic offense to meet King Yama, leaving behind as well a reputation for being 'rich but unkind' in this society.
